Just a thought that occurred to me. Ideally, in a free market people vote with their dollar. If a company is doing something people disagree with, they can take their money elsewhere.

What happens though when a company gets so large and the population gets so large that say a company has 5 million customers annually and does something that really upsets a large portion of that base, say 300,000.

The ability and likelihood hood of getting a group of people together for a political cause becomes more and more difficult the more people there are. This means there comes a point where a company could become so large they are effectively immune to backlash given how many people would need to organize to make a dent.
A thought about free markets, boycotts, and population

There are lots of very large companies - but how many of them are more than 100 years old?

They get big, get complacent, and then disappear. Because they are big, they are often out of communication with their own customers, and usually don't immediately recognize when they are in trouble. More often than not, by the time they do realize it, it is too late.

This is Google right now - having just alienated half the nation... not yet realizing what they have done. There is a time lag for the numbers to come in - and managers will be spinning those numbers to hide the problems.

As long as they keep competitively providing widgets to the other 4.7MM, they're technically providing a huge service to the society. As they accumulate more pissed-off subsets, there'll be growing interest in supporting their competition. Also, the founders and early employees that made the company great will eventually move on or die out.

I think we should spend more time thinking about how to prevent nepotism/dynasties of heirs who have less merit than their forebears and allow the nouveau riche to keep more of their income.

It is an interesting property of e.g., democracies... the larger the democracy, the larger the oppressed minority.
Ideally, the free market would prevent the company from even getting that large in the first place due to competition. But when this happens, a corporatocracy is imminent.
